channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] PHP2Shell becomes confirmed break-ins: a suspected China-nexus actor got root on about two dozen exposed PAN-OS firewalls — and OT vendors keep finding the same flaws in their own products
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 said on 29 October that it had independently verified research by Dream showing an attacker chaining the two PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation bug to get root through internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces. As reported by The Record, Cybersecurity Dive and Infosecurity Magazine on 29–30 October, Dream says a suspected China-nexus actor rooted about two dozen PAN-OS firewalls and management servers on 23–24 October, in the United States — among them a US government-affiliated network — Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, and then went after Active Directory credentials. The attribution is Dream’s; Unit 42 names no actor. Dream identifies the kernel bug as CVE-2026-46300, which CISA added to KEV on 28 October with a note that it can be chained with the PHP flaws to plant web shells and run commands as root (see the kernel flaw). Palo Alto says about 0.02% of its installed base had internet-facing management interfaces that were impacted, that it contacted each of those customers, and that patched devices are not affected because the fixes break the chain. Its advisory, Critical since 27 October and scored CVSS v4.0 9.2 (5.2 when management access is limited to a jump box), covers PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama through the management web interface and XML API; GlobalProtect portals and gateways are not affected, and by 29 October hotfixes were out for every supported branch. Siemens’ SSA-566512 for RUGGEDCOM APE1808, which runs PAN-OS, went to V1.1 on 28 October as an administrative revision; remediation is still through Siemens customer support together with Palo Alto’s workarounds, and no APE1808 exploitation has been reported. No oil and gas or OT victim has been named. Meanwhile OT vendors keep finding the same PHP flaws in their own products: Schneider Electric has added the EcoStruxure Foxboro DCS H90 Server, with no fix (see Foxboro DCS), and Siemens and ABB now list grid-control software, RTUs and cellular gateways (see OT vendor products). The sector read is ours: PAN-OS firewalls and Panorama commonly sit at refinery, gas-plant and pipeline IT/OT boundaries, the APE1808 puts the same software on RUGGEDCOM routers at field sites, and an attacker with root on the boundary firewall and domain credentials from behind it holds exactly the position segmentation is meant to deny. - Palo Alto Networks advisory for CVE-2026-109618 (published 21 Oct 2026, Critical since 27 Oct, last updated 29 Oct) and Unit 42 threat brief (29 Oct 2026), both reviewed directly; Dream research as reported by The Record (29 Oct 2026), Cybersecurity Dive and Infosecurity Magazine (30 Oct 2026); outlets give slightly different counts, so we say about two dozen; China-nexus attribution is Dream’s; Siemens ProductCERT SSA-566512 (V1.1, 28 Oct 2026); CISA KEV catalog 2026.10.30; CVSS v4.0 per Palo Alto; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - PHP fixes 21 Oct 2026; root compromises 23–24 Oct; KEV additions 26 and 28 Oct; last hotfixes and Unit 42 verification 29 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Microsoft ties the ConnectWise cloud compromise to China-aligned Storm-0940, which used the vendor’s own app identities to reach Microsoft 365 tenants — energy and chemicals are on its target list
item.category: Incident — Supply-chain compromise of a managed-service cloud app; China-state aligned actor per Microsoft; energy and chemicals among targeted sectors; no OT impact reported
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence wrote on 21 October that it assesses Storm-0940, an actor it calls China-state aligned, was responsible for the recently disclosed compromise of ConnectWise’s cloud services. The attacker gained control of the identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications, ConnectWise Cloud Backup among them, and used their stolen credentials to sign in to customers’ Microsoft 365 tenants as the trusted app, so the users’ multi-factor authentication never came into play. Microsoft says Storm-0940 drove the campaign with ARTEX, an open-source penetration-testing framework that can use any AI model, and that more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants received sign-in attempts — attempts, not compromises. Huntress says it saw unauthorised sign-ins at 162 tenants it monitors. A separate password spray from 10 to 14 October produced no successful sign-in. Once inside, it ran directory reconnaissance, added credentials to applications and changed roles and groups. ConnectWise, which says it first detected the activity on 14 October, suspended Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick), took its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services offline and disabled the affected app identities, and says it has seen no indication so far that partner backup data was compromised; its chief executive said on 22 October that services will be restored in controlled phases. Microsoft lists aerospace and defence, chemicals, energy, manufacturing and government among the targeted sectors; it names no victims, and no OT impact has been reported. The sector read is ours: a Microsoft 365 tenant holds the email, SharePoint libraries and Teams channels where plant drawings, network diagrams, vendor remote-access details and incident plans tend to live, and many operators and their contractors buy backup through managed service providers. - Microsoft Threat Intelligence blog (21 Oct 2026, updated 23 Oct); ConnectWise service actions as reported by BleepingComputer, and its detection date and phased-restoration statement as reported by Cybersecurity Dive (22 Oct 2026); unauthorised sign-in count per Huntress; other published counts conflict and are not given here; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Activity detected by ConnectWise 14 Oct 2026; Microsoft attribution 21 Oct 2026; restoration statement 22 Oct 2026; Microsoft blog updated 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] FBI and Secret Service: the FortiBleed credential campaign against FortiGate firewalls is still running — and the energy sector is among its targets
item.category: Active campaign — FBI and Secret Service warning on FortiGate credential theft; energy among targeted sectors; no CVE; no OT compromise described
item.description: In a joint advisory dated Tuesday 6 October (JCSA-20261006-01), the FBI and US Secret Service warned that the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat, with attackers still scanning for devices they can log into using credentials obtained earlier. There is no CVE: the agencies describe abuse of reused or leaked credentials and of legacy SHA-256 password storage. Researcher reporting adds credential stuffing and spraying from leak dumps, offline cracking of extracted hashes and a tool, FortigateSniffer, that passively captures authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Intruders have created administrator accounts with names such as fortiAdmin, forticloud-sync and fgtsecure, and some owners were locked out after attackers reset or deleted the legitimate accounts. The agencies say targets span all 16 US critical infrastructure sectors, energy and food and agriculture among them, and the FBI links the access to Payload ransomware; SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments that began this way. SOCRadar’s figure of 86,644 working device credentials in 194 countries dates from 19 June and is not a new count. Researchers describe the operator as a Russian-speaking initial access broker whose buyers overlap with INC and Lynx affiliates; that is their assessment, not the agencies’. No OT system compromise has been described and no oil and gas victim named. The sector read is ours: FortiGate is one of the most common firewalls at the IT/OT boundary and at remote sites, so a working login on one is a step toward operations. - FBI and US Secret Service joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01 (6 Oct 2026), as reported by Cybersecurity Dive and The Hacker News (7 Oct 2026); ransomware counts, credential figures and the operator profile are SOCRadar and researcher assessments; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Campaign first documented June 2026; agency warning 6 Oct 2026; reported 7 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Bloomberg: hackers reached tanker VL Prosperity’s propulsion system — the FBI reports no disruption and no attacker is named
item.category: Incident — Confirmed network compromise of two US-bound energy tankers by foreign cyber actors, per the Coast Guard and FBI; propulsion-system access reported by Bloomberg, not confirmed on the record; no disruption
item.description: On 2 October Bloomberg, citing unnamed US officials, reported that FBI and Coast Guard investigators found hackers had accessed the propulsion system of the crude supertanker VL Prosperity as it neared the Texas coast this summer. Neither agency has confirmed that on the record, and how long the access lasted, or what it could control, is unknown. The FBI says it has no reports of operational disruption, vessel instability, danger to crews or environmental harm. The confirmed part dates from September: cyber teams boarded two foreign-flagged, US-bound energy tankers in August after signs their networks were compromised, which the Coast Guard attributes to foreign cyber actors. Per Dragos, VL Prosperity was boarded on 21 August in the Atlantic and the second, unnamed tanker on 24 August. As of 31 October no new official statement or substantive new reporting had been found; the most recent substantive coverage dates from 5 October. For terminal operators, the exposure is the ship-shore interface. - Bloomberg report of 2 Oct 2026, as syndicated by gCaptain and SupplyChainBrain, citing unnamed US officials, with the FBI’s on-record statement; joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement via CyberScoop and The Record; Rear Adm. Grable via CBS News; boarding dates and VL Prosperity’s boarding location per Dragos (“VL Prosperity: What MTSA Cybersecurity Already Requires”, 24 Sep 2026); engine-room claims trace to Iranian state media and are unverified; the second vessel has not been named by the agencies - Boardings 21 and 24 Aug 2026; publicly confirmed 16 Sep 2026; Dragos commentary 24 Sep 2026; Bloomberg propulsion-system report 2 Oct 2026, not confirmed on the record; latest substantive coverage found 5 Oct 2026; no new official statement found to 31 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] CenterPoint Energy tells Texas its customer-data breach reached 1,062,060 residents — and still says gas and electric operations were not affected
item.category: Incident — Customer data breach at a gas and electric utility, now more than 1 million Texans; no operational impact
item.description: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based electric and natural gas utility, has told the Texas Attorney General’s Office that 1,062,060 Texas residents were affected by the breach it disclosed in September, SecurityWeek reported on 15 October. As SecurityWeek describes the filing, the exposed data includes names, addresses, Social Security numbers and driver’s licence numbers; residents of Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio may also be affected, and no overall total has been given. The company again says the incident did not affect its operations. In its SEC filing CenterPoint said an unauthorised party obtained customer information through one of its external-facing systems and that it learned of the breach from the actor’s own public post; BleepingComputer reported in September that the system was a public API with no rate limiting, web application firewall or automated access controls. The actor claimed nearly 7.5 million records and posted a 2.5 GB archive on 12 September; the company has not confirmed that figure, and class-action filings allege the intrusion ran from 17 August to 1 September. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one, and it is scored that way. It belongs on an oil and gas page because gas distribution utilities run customer-facing APIs alongside SCADA for pressure and flow, and the useful question is how much those two estates share. - CenterPoint Energy filing with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, as reported by SecurityWeek (15 Oct 2026); SEC filing and API detail as reported by BleepingComputer and The Record in September; record count claimed by the actor, not confirmed by the company - Intrusion alleged 17 Aug–1 Sep 2026; company disclosure 15 Sep 2026; Texas filing reported 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Engie says customer data was taken through a tool its partners use to market energy offers in France — its own IT systems were not compromised and no operations were affected
item.category: Incident — Customer data taken through a partner marketing tool at an energy supplier in France; Engie says its own IT was not compromised; no operational impact
item.description: Engie has told customers in France that it found unusual data-access activity in a tool that partners use to prospect for customers and market its energy offers. It cut off the access, says the breach is contained, and says its internal IT systems were not compromised. The exposed fields are names, postal and email addresses, phone numbers, the PDL and PCE supply-point identifiers used for electricity and gas connections, customer IDs and contract numbers; Engie says no banking data was involved. It has not said how many customers were affected or when the access was detected, and no group has claimed the breach. No operational or OT impact is reported, and this edition scores it as an IT-side incident. The sector read is ours: a gas supply-point number, a contract number and a name together make a convincing pretext for utility-themed phishing and for social engineering of call centres, and a partner’s marketing platform is a third-party path into customer data that suppliers rarely watch as closely as their own systems. - Engie statement and customer notification as reported by BleepingComputer (27 Oct 2026) and Infosecurity Magazine (28 Oct 2026); no customer count published; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Disclosed 27 Oct 2026; reported 27–28 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] AVEVA says intruders reached its corporate SharePoint — it reports that its software and production environments are separate and unaffected, and has named no impact on customers
item.category: Incident — Unauthorised access to an OT software vendor’s corporate document repository; AVEVA says its software and production environments are separate and unaffected; no customer impact reported
item.description: AVEVA has posted a notice, AVEVA-2026-007, on its cyber-security updates page saying it is investigating unauthorised access to its internal corporate SharePoint document repository. The entry carries no date; the page was last published on 23 October, so the notice was up by then. AVEVA says its software and production environments are separate from that repository and were not affected, that it has activated its incident response plan, brought in outside cybersecurity experts and notified law enforcement, and that it will notify third parties if the investigation finds a material impact on them. It gives no technical detail, no timeline and no action for customers, and we found no claim of responsibility and no press coverage. This is a vendor’s IT incident, not an OT one, and it is scored low. It is on this page because AVEVA’s software is common in the sector — its own 2026 security updates have covered Enterprise SCADA, Pipeline Simulation and Pipeline Integrity Monitor — and the useful question for operators is what their engineers and integrators have shared with the vendor (editorial assessment): support cases, project files and network details tend to travel through exactly this kind of document repository. - AVEVA notice AVEVA-2026-007 on its cyber-security updates page (undated; page last published 23 Oct 2026), reviewed directly; no press coverage found; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Notice posted by 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Lumen: Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” network of throwaway relays has carried attacks on SD-WAN, remote-management and IT-management platforms since 2023 — energy is on the target list, but no OT intrusion is described
item.category: Threat Intelligence — China state-sponsored group’s relay network used to exploit management and control-plane platforms; energy named among targeted sectors; no victim named; no OT intrusion described
item.description: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs published research on 28 October on what it calls Silent Train, a framework Volt Typhoon has used since about November 2023 to gain and keep access to the management and control-plane systems organisations depend on. It builds rapidly rotating chains of compromised home-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise equipment — more than 27 device classes — uses each chain for a target and then cleans up; CyberScoop reports one chain was assembled in under two minutes. Through it, Lumen says, the group exploited management platforms with zero-days: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN CVE-2026-20127 (CVSS v3.1 10.0 per Cisco, in KEV since 25 February), VeloCloud Orchestrator CVE-2026-16812 (in KEV since 27 July), N-able N-central CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 (in KEV since August 2025), Versa Director and, with moderate confidence, Quest KACE. These are earlier flaws than the Catalyst SD-WAN and VeloCloud bugs on this page’s cards (see Cisco SD-WAN Manager and VeloCloud); Lumen does not tie those to the group, but the same platforms keep being targeted. Lumen says it has notified hundreds of victims over about three years and lists water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation and emergency services among the critical infrastructure affected; one of its maps notes that the targeted states host assets tied to the country’s energy generation. It names no victim, confirms no energy-generation victim and describes no access to industrial control systems. Zero Day reports that Hawaii, California and Texas were recurring focal points, that Lumen researcher Michael Horka describes the activity as a mix of pre-positioning and espionage, and that the actors often come back with stolen credentials. Lumen points defenders to the joint advisories AA24-038A and AA26-113A. The sector read is ours: SD-WAN orchestrators and remote-management and IT-management servers are what tie compressor and pump stations, terminals and field offices together, and the small routers at remote sites and in home offices are the kind of device Silent Train is built from. - Lumen Black Lotus Labs research (28 Oct 2026), reviewed directly; coverage by CyberScoop and Zero Day (28 Oct 2026); KEV dates from the CISA catalog via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; attribution and victim descriptions are Lumen’s; no US government statement on this report found; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Framework in use since about Nov 2023; report published 28 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] The FBI seizes domains behind Microscan and FishHub, China-linked tools whose targets included gas and power companies — no OT intrusion is described
item.category: Threat Intelligence — US seizure of China-linked scanning and phishing tooling; gas and power companies among named targets; no compromise of those targets confirmed
item.description: On 8 October the Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains used to run two tools: Microscan, a Python web application with more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, supported by a Mirai-variant IoT botnet, and FishHub, used for spear-phishing and malware delivery. US authorities tie the tooling to China-based Integrity Technology Group, the company sanctioned last year and linked to a 2024 botnet takedown. The attribution wording varies: CyberScoop calls the tools Flax Typhoon-linked, while Cybersecurity Dive says the company’s activity mimics that of the group tracked as Flax Typhoon rather than equating the two. Court documents, as Cybersecurity Dive reports them, list Microscan targets including a South Carolina power company, airports in Japan and Poland, a multinational NGO, and gas and power companies in Taiwan; FishHub was aimed at Taiwanese universities. None of those targets has been confirmed as compromised. A joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory accompanied the seizures, and CISA’s Chris Butera said China-affiliated actors continue to position themselves inside critical infrastructure networks, OT systems included. No operational impact is described. For oil and gas the link is direct rather than inferred: gas companies were on the target list of a state-linked scanning platform, and scanning is the stage that comes before access. - DOJ and FBI announcement and joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory, as reported by CyberScoop (8 Oct 2026) and Cybersecurity Dive (9 Oct 2026); target list from court documents as reported; attribution wording differs between outlets; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Seizures announced 8 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] SOCRadar finds an exposed server showing INC and The Gentlemen affiliates driving intrusions through AI agents, with a human approving each step — industrial firms are the largest group among 62 targets
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Ransomware affiliates running intrusions through an AI-agent framework; industrial and manufacturing firms are the largest target group; initial access via KEV-listed flaws; no OT impact reported
item.description: SOCRadar published research on 20 October, updated on 23 October, on an exposed server that held the working logs of a Russian-speaking operator working with INC and The Gentlemen ransomware affiliates. The logs show a kill-chain framework called Phantom running AI coding agents on commercial models, with a human approving each step. SOCRadar counts 62 named target organisations, 36 of them in the US; industrial and manufacturing companies are the largest share at about 16%, followed by healthcare and pharmaceuticals, and four of the targets later appeared on leak sites. According to the operator’s own records, which SOCRadar did not independently verify, initial access came through three flaws that are all in KEV: FortiClient EMS CVE-2026-35616, SimpleHelp CVE-2024-57727 and cPanel/WHM CVE-2026-41940. No OT impact is reported, and we do not reproduce target or leak-site names. The sector read is ours: remote-support tools such as SimpleHelp are common in contractor support for plants and field sites, and an operator working through known, listed flaws at machine speed shortens the time a defender has between a KEV listing and its use. - SOCRadar research (20 Oct 2026, updated 23 Oct 2026), with coverage by The Hacker News (23 Oct 2026); the exploited-flaw list comes from the operator’s records and was not verified by SOCRadar; KEV dates from the CISA catalog; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Published 20 Oct 2026; updated 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Insurer Resilience: ransomware was 9% of its energy and utility claims but about 70% of the losses — and none of the claims involved control-system manipulation
item.category: Research — Insurer claims data for energy and utilities; no control-system manipulation in any claim
item.description: Cyber insurer Resilience has published an analysis of the energy and utilities claims it received between January 2023 and early September 2026, reported by Industrial Cyber on 21 October. Ransomware made up about 9% of the sector’s claims, against 6% elsewhere in Resilience’s book, but drove about 70% of incurred losses. Email compromise was more common, at 21% of energy claims compared with 10% elsewhere, yet accounted for only 2% of losses; malware was 7% of claims. About 17% of energy claims began at a vendor, and roughly a third of those vendors were HR, payroll, benefits or accounting firms. Attackers got past multi-factor authentication by talking people out of one-time codes and by hijacking sessions, and clients with tested backups and segmentation recovered or kept production running. None of the energy claims, water and wastewater clients included, involved control-system manipulation; Resilience says claims data probably understates OT risk, because OT intrusions can go unnoticed. This is one insurer’s portfolio, not a census of the sector. The read for oil and gas is ours: the losses that land are business-side ransomware and the shutdowns it forces, so recovering the systems that schedule, measure and bill product matters as much as protecting the control network. - Resilience report “Cyber risk in energy and utilities: Lessons from Insurance Claims” as reported by Industrial Cyber (21 Oct 2026); claims period 1 Jan 2023 to 5 Sep 2026; oil and gas application is editorial assessment - Reported 21 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Securing the remote wellsite: an Industrial Cyber feature collects Dragos’s finding that oil and gas has the weakest IT/OT segmentation of any sector, and practitioners’ advice on vendor access
item.category: Research — Industry feature on securing upstream oil and gas; data from earlier in 2026; no new incident
item.description: Industrial Cyber published a feature on 20 October on securing upstream oil and gas operations across distance, remoteness and harsh environments. It reports no new incident or advisory, and its data come from earlier in 2026. It cites Dragos’s 2026 OT/ICS year in review: poor IT/OT segmentation appeared in 29% of Dragos’s oil and gas cases, the highest share of any sector, and the group Dragos tracks as VOLTZITE compromised cellular gateways across US oil and gas infrastructure before moving into engineering workstations. A Tosi survey of 100 US upstream and midstream OT leaders found 87% confident they could detect a breach within 24 hours, but only 16% credited continuous OT monitoring for that confidence. The practitioners quoted converge on remote access. Dragos’s Michael Hoffman points to legacy RTUs and radio networks built for reliability rather than authentication, and recommends MFA, brokered jump hosts and recorded, time-bound sessions. OMV Petrom’s Albert Vartic would limit remote control to predefined safe actions, keep shutdowns local and keep safety systems independent of networked control. Thales’s Edwin Loke warns of vendor “shadow access”, such as unmanaged 4G routers, at unattended sites. - Industrial Cyber feature by Anna Ribeiro (20 Oct 2026), citing Dragos’s 2026 OT/ICS year in review and a Tosi survey; the statistics are secondary and predate this edition’s window - Published 20 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Supermarket refrigeration attacks have spread from France to five more European countries — a food-sector campaign, and a test for every vendor-managed controller you expose
item.category: Cross-sector lesson — confirmed OT attacks on supermarket refrigeration controllers in France (Oct) and five more European countries (1–2 Nov), and a suspected one at US military commissaries; not an oil and gas incident; sector link is editorial assessment
item.description: Over the nights of 11–13 October, the second wave hitting stores with Dixell equipment, attackers remotely changed settings on web-managed refrigeration controllers in French supermarkets, forcing extended defrost cycles that pushed cabinets toward about 50°C and spoiled stock; the Paris prosecutor reports fires at some sites. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that roughly 700 of France’s 10,000 supermarkets were hit, across Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché and Netto, and Monoprix. CERT-FR’s alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland and Dixell xweb on 13 October, and on 16 October said the campaigns are probably still under way; as of 2 November CERT-FR had issued no later version, and no new attack nights, attribution or arrests had been reported in France since 13 October. On the night of 1–2 November a new wave hit supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia: Ahold Delhaize reported an “IT incident” affecting refrigeration at dozens of Delhaize stores, Colruyt said five franchised Spar shops were attacked, the contractor that runs Delhaize’s refrigeration said evaporators had been switched into defrost, ICA, Coop and Musgrave (SuperValu) reported affected stores, and in Estonia refrigeration supplier Kitman Coldtech said an older Danfoss controller was set to 50°C; no actor has been named and no authority has linked the wave to France. No actor has claimed it, no ransom has been demanded and the entry route has not been established; Danfoss and Copeland say most affected units are older, end-of-life models. Two follow-ups reach beyond retail. Nozomi Networks’ 13 October analysis links the same precondition — controllers left reachable from the internet for vendor management — to fuel automatic tank gauges, citing Shadowserver’s count of 909 exposed gauges in June. And Claroty Team82 reported on 13 October that an AI coding agent, redirected by a human, reproduced a previously disclosed Danfoss AK-SM 800A authentication-bypass and command-injection chain to root on a lab device in about 28 minutes for roughly $6; Team82 does not say those flaws were used in France. On 22 October Forescout counted 12,976 internet-exposed refrigeration management service observations on 6,017 IP addresses in 99 countries — services, not devices. On 29 October Reuters, citing four unnamed officials, reported that US investigators are treating freezer failures at at least six military commissaries since late August, where units switched to defrost and stock spoiled, as a suspected cyberattack; Army and Air Force investigators and US Cyber Command are involved, one official said investigators had spoken to French police, and the Pentagon has confirmed neither unauthorised access nor a cause. Reuters could not establish whether the stores used Danfoss equipment, though records for one, at Naval Air Facility El Centro, list a Danfoss control system. This is not an oil and gas incident and it does not count toward this page’s score. The lesson is ours: tank gauges, forecourt and convenience-store refrigeration, building management and vendor-monitored packages at terminals and retail fuel sites belong to the same exposure class. - CERT-FR alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 (v1 12 Oct, v2 13 Oct, v3 16 Oct 2026); Finance Minister Lescure via AP (13 Oct 2026); affected chains per SecurityWeek (15 Oct 2026); Nozomi Networks analysis and Claroty Team82 research (13 Oct 2026); Forescout Vedere Labs exposure count (22 Oct 2026); US commissary investigation per Reuters (29 Oct 2026), via The Next Web; exposure counts are third-party figures; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment; Reuters, CBS News/AFP, RTÉ and ERR (2 Nov 2026) for the new wave - Attacks on the nights of 11–13 Oct 2026; CERT-FR alert updated 16 Oct 2026, no later version as of 2 Nov; new wave in five more countries 1–2 Nov 2026; Forescout count 22 Oct 2026; US commissary investigation reported 29 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Dragos: old worms such as Conficker, Sality and WannaCry keep turning up in OT incident calls — and the wrong cleanup can do more harm than the infection
item.category: Research — Commodity malware in OT networks and how to clean it up; vendor guidance, no actor
item.description: Dragos’s Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff wrote on 15 October that requests for help with legacy commodity infections — Sality, Gammima, WannaCry and Conficker among them — have risen sharply in recent years. Many OT networks Dragos is called into carry between 20 and 70 distinct commodity-malware variants spread across several subnets, often on systems older than Windows XP SP2. They put the rise down to more networking and remote access, better visibility, and regulation that expects critical-infrastructure networks to be clean. Their answer is a triage framework they call Now, Next and Never, published with a white paper, and a warning that a cleanup done the wrong way can be riskier than the infection it is meant to remove. There is no CVE and no actor here. The fit for oil and gas is our assessment and an easy one: refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres keep operator stations, historians and vendor PCs on old Windows builds for years, and an aggressive cleanup — mass reboots, forced updates or an endpoint agent pushed onto running units — can stop a process the worm never touched. - Dragos blog by Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff (15 Oct 2026), with its linked white paper; oil and gas application is editorial assessment - Published 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Symantec: the China-nexus group behind Warlock ransomware broke into a water utility and a telecom operator through on-premises SharePoint — no OT impact is described, and no energy victim is named
item.category: Threat Intelligence — China-nexus ransomware intrusions via SharePoint; water and telecom victims; cross-sector context, no OT impact described
item.description: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team reported on 1 October that a group it calls Longlegs, which it describes as a China-nexus threat actor also tracked as Storm-2603, has attacked at least four organisations in the past two months: two critical infrastructure operators — a water utility and a telecommunications provider — plus a regional government body and a university, in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries in Europe, Africa and Latin America. No victim or country is named. Symantec says the group typically gets in by exploiting several vulnerabilities in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server; the CVEs it names are the 2025 ToolShell flaws (CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771), alongside unspecified related SharePoint flaws. Once inside, the group steals ASP.NET machine keys, sideloads DLLs, uses Visual Studio Code tunnels and NetExec, and loads a vulnerable signed driver (CVE-2025-1055 in K7RKScan) to switch off security tools; in one intrusion Symantec documents, Warlock was pushed to at least 33 hosts through SYSVOL. Symantec does not describe any operational or OT impact at the water utility and does not say ransomware was deployed there. It is on this page as cross-sector context, not an oil and gas incident: the targets are critical infrastructure operators, the entry point is the kind of on-premises collaboration server that engineering and document-control teams often run, and machine-key theft means a server patched after compromise can still be reopened. - Symantec Threat Hunter Team report, with coverage by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek; attribution and victim descriptions are Symantec’s; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Published 1 Oct 2026; intrusions over the preceding two months

item.title: [High] PHP2Shell in OT products: Siemens now lists Spectrum Power and Energy Engage as affected, and ABB has no fix yet for its Netcontrol RTUs — while its obsolete Arctic wireless gateways will never get one
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited PHP flaws in OT vendor products: Siemens grid-control and energy software, ABB RTUs and wireless gateways; CISA KEV; several products have no fix, and one line never will
item.description: Siemens’ SSA-166980, which previously listed only Smart Infrastructure products that were not affected, now lists affected ones. Version 1.2, published on 29 October, adds the Spectrum Power family — Siemens’ grid control (EMS/SCADA) software — together with AMIS TS, blueplanet 360 and Energy Engage. Fix status varies by product. Spectrum Power 7 (IHM with NagiosXI) takes Red Hat’s PHP patch for RHEL 8 and 9; Spectrum Power 3 (IHM with NagiosXI on RHEL 7) is affected by CVE-2026-109619 only and also takes Red Hat’s patch; Spectrum Power TG’s Windows WebConsole and WebQuery components need PHP upgraded to 8.5.12; and Energy Engage V3.1SP1 needs PHP 8.1.34 release 6. There is no fix for Spectrum Power 4’s Nagios and Zabbix, Web Office Portal V3.0–3.2 and HISViews V1.0 components, for AMIS TS or for blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISX, and none is planned for Energy Engage V2.0SP9. Siemens scores the two flaws CVSS v3.1 9.8 and 8.1. Building products such as Desigo, Climatix, Siveillance and SiPass remain listed as not affected, Siemens’ software-product advisory SSA-566435 still lists no affected products, and Siemens reports no exploitation of any of its products. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-166980 (V1.2, 29 Oct 2026) and SSA-566435; ABB advisories 2NGA003256 and 2NGA003224 (30 Oct 2026) and the ASPECT advisory (29 Oct 2026), via ABB’s alerts page and CSAF records; ABB/B&R SA26P015 (last revised 23 Oct 2026); Rockwell SD1802; Moxa MPSA-260001 (22 Oct 2026); Cisco cisco-sa-php-october26-Jj384Daq (v1.10, 30 Oct 2026), reviewed directly; Johnson Controls JCI-PSA-2026-24 (v5, 30 Oct 2026); WaterISAC PHP2Shell notice (updated 29 Oct 2026); CISA KEV catalog 2026.10.30; OT relevance is editorial assessment - PHP fixes 21 Oct 2026; KEV addition 26 Oct; Siemens SSA-166980 V1.2 and ABB ASPECT advisory 29 Oct; ABB Netcontrol and Arctic advisories, Cisco advisory v1.10 and Johnson Controls v5 30 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Schneider Electric adds the EcoStruxure Foxboro DCS H90 Server to its PHP2Shell bulletin — there is no fix, and the only mitigation is blocking two HPE server-management ports
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited PHP flaws listed for a DCS server; mitigation only, no fix; the PHP CVEs are in CISA KEV; no exploitation of Schneider products reported
item.description: Schneider Electric revised security bulletin SESB-2026-295-01 to version 3.0.0 on 28 October to add the EcoStruxure Foxboro DCS H90 Server, running on HPE ProLiant DL380 Gen9 hardware with Windows Server 2016, as affected by the PHP2Shell flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. No fix is listed. The mitigation is to confirm at the firewall that TCP ports 2301 and 2381 are blocked; Schneider says those ports are used by HPE System Management Homepage, so the exposure appears to sit in the server’s management layer rather than in the control software itself (our reading; the bulletin does not name the component). Versions 3.1.0 and 3.2.0, on 29 and 30 October, added no products and changed no remediation. The rest of the bulletin stands: EcoStruxure Control Engineering has had remediation since version 2.0.0 (26 October), applied automatically when the virtual machine can reach the debian.org and sury.org repositories and otherwise as a dedicated patch from Schneider; the Security Expert web client is fixed in 1.48.4.0; and LINEoptimize, formerly Plant iT LMS, is remediated through ProLeiT support. Schneider cites the PHP security team’s CVSS v4.0 9.2 for both flaws, which CISA added to KEV on 26 October, and the bulletin reports no exploitation of Schneider products. Exploitation elsewhere is confirmed, against PAN-OS firewalls (see the top story). The sector read is ours: Foxboro DCS runs refinery, gas-processing and petrochemical units, a DCS server such as the H90 typically sits inside the control network rather than at its edge, and a server-management web service is easy to miss when firewall rules were written around the DCS application. - Schneider Electric security bulletin SESB-2026-295-01 (v1.0.0 22 Oct; v2.0.0 26 Oct; v3.0.0 28 Oct; current v3.2.0, 30 Oct 2026, with no changes since v3.0.0), reviewed directly; CVSS v4.0 per the PHP security team as cited by Schneider; CISA KEV catalog 2026.10.30; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Foxboro DCS H90 Server added 28 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] The Linux kernel flaw used to turn PHP2Shell web shells into root is in KEV, due 31 October — and Siemens lists it in the Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 CPU 1518(F)-4 PN/DP MFP
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited Linux kernel privilege escalation used to turn PHP2Shell footholds into root; CISA KEV; also listed for the Linux subsystem of a Siemens S7-1500 CPU
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel flaw reported as “Fragnesia”, to KEV on 28 October with a 31 October federal deadline. When the kernel coalesces network buffers it can drop the marker that says a memory fragment is shared, so ESP decryption may write in place over page-cache data; Red Hat describes the result as a low-privileged local user being able to write into the page cache of read-only files, and scores it CVSS v3.1 7.8. It needs local access, so it is a second-stage flaw: CISA’s entry says it can be chained with the PHP2Shell flaws to implant PHP web shells and run commands as root, and Dream’s research names it as the kernel bug used to root PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October (see the top story). Fixes are in upstream stable kernels 5.10.257, 5.15.208, 6.1.174, 6.6.141, 6.12.91, 6.18.33 and 7.0.10, and in Red Hat kernel updates for RHEL 8, 9 and 10.2. The OT bridge is Siemens: its advisories SSA-019113 and SSA-082556 and its data in the CVE record list the optional Linux subsystem of the SIMATIC S7-1500 CPU 1518-4 PN/DP MFP and 1518F-4 PN/DP MFP, and the SIPLUS variant, as affected. Firmware V3.1.6 is fixed by V3.1.7; V3.1.5, which Siemens no longer maintains, has no fix, and Siemens advises running only trusted applications and restricting access to the Linux subsystem’s shell. No exploitation of the Siemens CPUs has been reported. The sector read is ours: firewalls, gateways, HMIs and edge devices across plants and field sites run Linux kernels their owners rarely see, and a local root bug is what turns any web-shell foothold on them into full control. - CISA KEV entry (catalog 2026.10.30) and the CVE record via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup, including Red Hat’s CVSS and Siemens’ product data; Siemens ProductCERT SSA-019113 and SSA-082556; PAN-OS chain per Dream as reported by Infosecurity Magazine (30 Oct 2026); OT relevance is editorial assessment - CVE published 23 May 2026; added to KEV 28 Oct 2026 (due 31 Oct)

item.title: [Critical] Ivanti Connect Secure: CISA adds the root-escalation link and a third chained flaw to KEV — and a build that fixes CVE-2026-104935 may not close the chain
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited VPN zero-day chain; three chained CVEs now in CISA KEV; fix status for the root-escalation flaw not confirmed
item.description: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that a limited number of Connect Secure customers had been attacked through a chain of flaws that gives an unauthenticated attacker root on a fully patched appliance. Two of them, an authentication bypass by spoofing and a file write, are fixed under CVE-2026-104935, which Ivanti scores CVSS v3.1 8.6; the fixed releases are 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1, and CISA added it to KEV on 13 October. On 30 October CISA added two more Connect Secure flaws and says both can be chained with CVE-2026-104935. CVE-2026-111357, whose record MITRE published on 15 October, is a privilege escalation to root in which the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data; MITRE scores it CVSS v3.1 7.0, Canada’s Cyber Centre listed it as exploited in an update of 16 October, and its federal deadline is 2 November. CVE-2026-118527, which CISA’s catalog lists as a predictable-identifier flaw (generation of predictable numbers or identifiers), is due on 13 November; we found no published description or score for it. Earlier editions of this card said the privilege-escalation link had no CVE; that was wrong, because CVE-2026-111357 has had a record since 15 October and CISA now ties it to the chain. Fix status is not confirmed: NVD lists Connect Secure up to 22.8R2.5 and 25.1.x before 25.1.1.3 as affected by CVE-2026-111357, so 22.8R2.5 should not be assumed to fix the whole chain — check Ivanti’s advisory for the build that fixes it. Volexity found the chain during an incident response and tracks the actor as UTA0576, with only low confidence that the motive is criminal rather than espionage; its case began on 3 October, and Defused saw activity from 1 October. The intruders left no web shell, ran commands through the exploit itself, took domain credentials stored on the appliance, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, and wiped logs; Volexity and CISA warn that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect the compromise. No oil and gas victim has been named. The sector read is ours: Connect Secure is a common front door for engineers and vendors into OT DMZs, and this chain hands an outsider the domain credentials behind it. - Ivanti advisory for CVE-2026-104935 and Volexity research (13 Oct 2026), as reported by SecurityWeek, CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive; Defused observations via Cybersecurity Dive; CISA KEV catalog 2026.10.30; CVE-2026-111357 record and NVD configuration via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; Canadian Centre for Cyber Security AV26-1035 (update of 16 Oct 2026); Ivanti’s advisory could not be read this run; OT remote-access relevance is editorial assessment - Exploitation from at least early October 2026; CVE-2026-104935 disclosed and added to KEV 13 Oct; CVE-2026-111357 record published 15 Oct; CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 added to KEV 30 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Cisco ASA and FTD: an exploited zero-day lets an unauthenticated attacker reload the firewall through its remote-access VPN when secondary authentication is configured — in KEV with a 1 November deadline
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited zero-day in the remote-access VPN of a common boundary firewall; denial of service; CISA KEV; no workaround
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 on 28 October for CVE-2026-76418 in Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) software. When the SSL remote-access VPN login service is reachable and a tunnel group is configured with a secondary authentication server group, a crafted request can make the device reload, and the attacker does not need to log in. Cisco tells administrators to check every tunnel group, including DefaultWEBVPNGroup. It scores the flaw CVSS v3.1 8.6, says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October, and says there are no workarounds; the mitigation it describes, disabling secondary authentication, removes a layer of VPN security. The first fixed releases are ASA 9.16.4.104, 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48, and 9.24.1.27 or 9.24.10.1, and FTD 7.0.11, 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1; Cisco’s cloud-delivered firewall and firewall management, Secure Access and Secure Firewall Management Center software are not affected. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 29 October with a 1 November federal deadline. Cisco has not described the attackers, the number of targets or any follow-on activity, and this is a denial-of-service flaw, not code execution. No oil and gas victim is named. The sector read is ours: ASA and FTD are common at IT/OT boundaries and as the remote-access VPN that engineers and vendors use to reach plants and pipelines, secondary authentication is exactly the extra factor many OT access designs add, and a firewall that can be made to reload on demand takes vendor access and boundary logging down with it. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 (v1.0, 28 Oct 2026), reviewed directly; CISA KEV catalog 2026.10.30; CVSS v3.1 per Cisco; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Advisory published 28 Oct 2026; added to KEV 29 Oct 2026 (due 1 Nov)

item.title: [Critical] BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, exploited since late August by a suspected China-nexus espionage group, is now in KEV — CISA set a 19 October deadline for federal agencies
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-support appliance zero-day exploited by a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor; in CISA KEV since 16 Oct
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-102764, a flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support, to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline, a day after Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reported that it had been exploited as a zero-day from late August. GTIG attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, on the strength of tooling and technique overlap. The flaw is improper validation of message origins in Remote Support’s internal messaging, which lets an attacker carry out file operations on the appliance; BeyondTrust scores it CVSS v4.0 9.3, and every Remote Support release up to 26.2.3 is affected. SecurityWeek reports that two appliances were compromised, one hosted by BeyondTrust and one self-hosted. The intruders gained root, installed a PHP web shell GTIG calls SAWFLY and a SOCKS5 tunneller it calls BARECLAW, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the product’s own file-transfer feature to pull documents from user desktops. BeyondTrust identified the defect on 28 September, shipped patch BT26-05-RS on 8 October for releases 24.3.1 to 26.2.3, and had patched all SaaS customers by 9 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand, and releases older than 24.3.1 must upgrade first. GTIG names no victims or sectors and advises treating any internet-reachable appliance that ran a vulnerable release during the window as potentially compromised. The sector read is ours: remote-support tools are how many IT help desks, OEMs and integrators reach operator stations and engineering PCs, so a compromised support appliance is a ready-made path to the plant side. - Google Threat Intelligence Group blog (15 Oct 2026); BeyondTrust advisory BT26-05; CISA KEV entry (added 16 Oct 2026); compromise and timeline details as reported by SecurityWeek and The Record (16 Oct 2026); CVSS from the CVE record; OT relevance is editorial assessment - Exploited from late August 2026; defect identified 28 Sep; fix shipped 8 Oct, SaaS patched 9 Oct; disclosed 15 Oct; added to KEV 16 Oct 2026 (due 19 Oct)

item.title: [Critical] Citrix NetScaler: a fourth critical flaw (CVSS 9.5) follows three exploited ones — and builds that fixed the zero-days stay exposed when used as a SAML identity provider
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access gateway; three exploited flaws in CISA KEV and a fourth critical flaw patched 8 Oct
item.description: On 8 October Citrix published bulletin CTX697191 for CVE-2026-107406, a memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider, which Citrix says may lead to remote code execution or denial of service. It is scored CVSS v4.0 9.5, has no workaround, and Citrix says it is not aware of exploitation; it was still not in KEV as of CISA’s 30 October catalog. The catch is that builds which fixed the late-September zero-days — 14.1-73.37 to 73.41 and 13.1-64.23 to 64.28 — remain vulnerable when the appliance acts as a SAML identity provider, and older builds are vulnerable in either role, so many sites must upgrade again, to 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29 and later (13.1-37.283 for FIPS and NDcPP). The three earlier flaws are confirmed exploited and in KEV. CVE-2026-88771, unauthenticated command execution, and CVE-2026-88772, a memory overflow that needs DTLS (on by default on VPN virtual servers), both CVSS v4 9.5, were patched and listed on 27 September. CVE-2026-88779, a SAML memory overflow scored 8.7, was patched on 3 October and listed on 4 October; Citrix and watchTowr describe it as a crash bug, and CISA has warned it is used to force reboots so that code planted through 88771 runs. CISA has renewed its call to patch and released Sigma detection rules. Google Threat Intelligence and LevelBlue describe what intruders leave behind: a PHP web shell (WHIPSHOT), a Python tunneller (SLAPSHOT), a rogue superuser account named sec_monitor and stolen configuration archives. Mandiant describes dozens of victim organisations across North America and Europe and suspected state-nexus actors, unnamed; Arctic Wolf counts at least 78 targeted organisations, which is not a count of confirmed compromises; Shadowserver sees more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. Upgrading does not remove an intruder who is already in. No oil and gas victim has been named. The sector read is ours: NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for vendor and engineer remote access into refinery, gas-plant and pipeline OT DMZs. - Citrix bulletins CTX697096, CTX697174 and CTX697191; CISA KEV entries and alerts; CVE-2026-107406 record and fixed builds via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup and The Hacker News (9 Oct 2026); CISA’s renewed warning via Cybersecurity Dive (12 Oct 2026); post-exploitation findings from Google Threat Intelligence and LevelBlue; victim and exposure counts from Mandiant, Arctic Wolf and Shadowserver; OT remote-access relevance is editorial assessment - Two zero-days patched and added to KEV 27 Sep 2026; third flaw patched 3 Oct, added to KEV 4 Oct; fourth flaw disclosed 8 Oct 2026; CISA renewed its patch call, reported 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] KEV, 13–15 October: an exploited PAN-OS root flaw, a CVSS 9.8 Cisco email-gateway bug and the Windows zero-day from Patch Tuesday, all on three-day deadlines
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA KEV additions 13–15 Oct: boundary firewall, mail gateway and Windows zero-days
item.description: CISA added seven CVEs to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog between 13 and 15 October; Ivanti’s has its own card. The one closest to OT is CVE-2026-0322 in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS, added on 14 October: an attacker with credentials and network access to the management interface of a PA-Series or VM-Series firewall or Panorama can run code as root. Palo Alto, which found it internally, reports very limited exploitation, scores it CVSS v4.0 8.6 and lists fixed releases including 12.2.4, 12.1.10-h2, 11.2.16, 11.1.16-h3 and 10.2.18-h12; Prisma Access and Cloud NGFW are not affected. Also on 14 October came CVE-2026-76519 in Cisco Secure Email Gateway, CVSS 9.8: a sender with no login can write files and reach root through a crafted attachment where File Reputation is enabled on a mail policy and Content Scanner Tools are older than 25.3.0.5525. Cisco is aware of attacks this month; the fixes are AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 or 16.5.0-780 (the 16.0 train must migrate) or the Content Scanner Tools update. It is separate from CVE-2026-76461, a SQL-injection flaw in the same gateway that was exploited and added to KEV in September. On 13 October CISA listed CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell security-feature bypass (CVSS 8.8) that Microsoft’s October update fixed among more than 1,400 CVEs; SecurityWeek describes it as a Mark-of-the-Web bypass that needs a user to open a file. The rest were AhsayCBS backup-server flaws CVE-2026-105133 and -105134 (14 October) and Atlassian Data Center CVE-2026-21589 (15 October). Deadlines run from 16 to 18 October. No victims or actors are named for any of them. The sector read is ours: PAN-OS firewalls commonly sit at refinery and pipeline IT/OT boundaries, and Windows engineering workstations and HMIs are where a mail-borne file ends up. - CISA KEV catalog (version 2026.10.15); Palo Alto Networks advisory for CVE-2026-0322; Cisco advisory cisco-sa-esa-afw-zqYJkjxp as reported by The Hacker News and SecurityWeek; Microsoft’s October 2026 release as reported by SecurityWeek; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - KEV additions 13, 14 and 15 Oct 2026; deadlines 16–18 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] A Siemens Software Center flaw is being abused in a ClickFix malware campaign — CISA added it to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November deadline
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens’ software download and licensing app, abused in a ClickFix campaign; CISA KEV
item.description: Siemens Software Center, the Windows application that downloads, installs, activates and updates purchased Siemens software, loads DLLs from an uncontrolled search path. Tracked as CVE-2026-110936, the flaw lets an attacker who can place a crafted DLL where the program looks run code with its privileges; Siemens scores it CVSS v3.1 6.7 and v4.0 8.4. Siemens published advisory SSA-580366 on 15 October, added the fix on 17 October and on 19 October confirmed active exploitation: attackers are pairing a genuine, validly signed copy of the program (version 3.5.8.7) with their own DLLs, delivered in installer packages, as part of what Siemens calls the “Romulus” multi-platform ClickFix campaign, which tricks users into running commands themselves. Siemens says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached, names no final malware, and has published indicators and behavioural detections. Version 4.0.9.8 fixes the flaw, and existing installations update on their next start. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November deadline and republished the advisory as ICSA-26-295-03 on 22 October, listing energy among the affected sectors. Huntress reported the flaw. The sector read is ours: because the lure brings its own signed copy, patching installed copies does not by itself stop it, and application allow-listing that trusts anything Siemens-signed on engineering laptops and plant-office PCs may let it run. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-580366 (V1.0 15 Oct, V1.1 17 Oct, V1.2 19 Oct 2026) and Siemens ProductCERT post on active exploitation (19 Oct 2026); CISA KEV entry (20 Oct 2026) and ICSA-26-295-03 (22 Oct 2026); OT allow-listing relevance is editorial assessment - Advisory 15 Oct 2026; exploitation confirmed 19 Oct; added to KEV 20 Oct (due 3 Nov); CISA republication 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] The FortiOS flaw behind Unit 42’s Peerstitch case is in KEV — attackers inside a telecom MSP’s FortiManager reached root on managed FortiGates, and more than 500 firewall configurations were exposed
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited FortiOS privilege-escalation flaw used against a managed service provider’s FortiGates; CISA KEV
item.description: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 14 October on an intrusion at a telecommunications managed service provider. The attackers got in through FortiManager CVE-2024-47575, the 2024 “FortiJump” flaw in the protocol FortiManager uses to manage FortiGates, then used CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS command-line path traversal, to get root on managed firewalls, where they installed a loader Unit 42 calls PEERSTITCH and an SSH reverse-shell channel hidden in an Apache module. Configuration files, serial numbers and public addresses of more than 500 FortiGates the provider managed were taken; Unit 42 describes that as exposure of configuration and credential material, not confirmed intrusion into those customers’ networks. It tracks the activity as CL-STA-0954, which overlaps UNC5820, and names no state. CVE-2025-61624 was fixed in April 2026; Fortinet rates it Medium because it needs privileged, authenticated access, and now marks it known exploited. CISA added it to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October deadline. The CVE record also lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, an industrial appliance that can run FortiOS, as affected. The sector read is ours: many pipeline, terminal and field networks have FortiGates managed by a carrier or MSP, and those firewalls’ configurations are a map of the OT boundary. - Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 report (14 Oct 2026); Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-122; CISA KEV entry (16 Oct 2026); RUGGEDCOM APE1808 per the CVE record; no numeric score is given because published figures differ; OT relevance is editorial assessment - Fix released April 2026; Unit 42 report 14 Oct 2026; added to KEV 16 Oct 2026 (due 19 Oct)

item.title: [Medium] Fortinet has shipped fixes across FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator ahead of a 10 November disclosure — check versions now, because scanners will not flag them yet
item.category: Critical Advisory — Fortinet fixes released ahead of disclosure across FortiOS and management products; CVE details due 10 Nov; no exploitation known
item.description: Fortinet announced on 21 October, in a blog post by its chief information security officer, Carl Windsor, a security hardening release of critical and high-severity fixes for FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, with the advisories, CVE IDs and scores due on its PSIRT page on Patch Tuesday, 10 November. It says some of the fixes came from AI-assisted testing and urges customers to patch internet-facing devices first. The fixed releases are FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14; FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13; FortiMail 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9, with 7.2 users moving to 7.4 or later; and FortiAuthenticator 8.0.4 and 6.6.11. FortiSASE was updated automatically, and FortiManager Cloud may need a manual update. Australia’s ACSC issued a critical alert on 23 October, and WaterISAC’s TLP:CLEAR notification of 27 October sets out the concern, which is the gap: attackers can compare fixed and unfixed builds before 10 November, while scanners that work from CVE IDs will not flag affected devices until then, so versions have to be checked directly. No exploitation of these flaws has been reported. Our 28 October edition said no Fortinet source could be found and treated WaterISAC as the only source; Fortinet’s own post was available, and the fixed versions match. We still print no CVE or score until Fortinet publishes. WaterISAC also repeats that the FortiMail flaw CVE-2026-104286, already in KEV, is exploited (see FortiMail). The sector read is ours: FortiGate and FortiManager are common at oil and gas IT/OT boundaries and field sites, and a provider’s FortiManager has already proved a route to the firewalls it manages (see Peerstitch). - Fortinet blog post by CISO Carl Windsor (21 Oct 2026); ACSC alert and HKCERT bulletin (23 Oct 2026); WaterISAC TLP:CLEAR vulnerability notification (27 Oct 2026); no CVE or CVSS printed until Fortinet publishes; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Fortinet announcement 21 Oct 2026; builds shipped from 22 Oct; ACSC alert 23 Oct; WaterISAC notice 27 Oct 2026; Fortinet disclosure due 10 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] Arista’s third exploited VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day in four months is now in KEV — any logged-in tenant user can take operator control of the system that configures remote-site SD-WAN
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited SD-WAN orchestrator zero-day, the third in four months; in CISA KEV since 23 Oct
item.description: Arista disclosed CVE-2026-114625 on 22 October, a SQL injection in the on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) that lets any authenticated user, down to the lowest built-in tenant role, gain operator privileges, act as a local superuser operator and affect the VCO host. Arista scores it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4. Arista says it detected the flaw itself, that it is known to be actively exploited and that no configuration prevents the exposure, and it has published two attacker addresses. The fixes are 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12; hosted and dedicated orchestrators have already been patched, and VeloCloud gateways and edges are not affected. It is the third exploited VCO zero-day since July, after CVE-2026-16812 (in KEV since 27 July) and September’s CVE-2026-93952 (in KEV since 22 September), so builds that fixed September’s flaw need upgrading again. CISA added it to KEV on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, which has now passed; our 23 October edition said it was not yet listed, which was incorrect. No victim or actor has been named. The sector read is ours: SD-WAN commonly links compressor and pump stations, terminals and field offices, and whoever holds the orchestrator can change routing, firewall and remote-access settings on every edge it manages. - Arista Security Advisory 0199 (22 Oct 2026), with coverage by SecurityWeek, The Hacker News and BleepingComputer (22–23 Oct 2026); CISA KEV catalog 2026.10.30; CVSS per Arista; earlier VCO flaws per CISA KEV; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Disclosed and patched 22 Oct 2026; added to KEV 23 Oct 2026 (due 26 Oct)

item.title: [High] SonicWall SMA1000: a CVSS 10 pre-authentication flaw drew exploitation attempts two days after the fix — no confirmed breach, not in KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access appliance, maximum-severity pre-authentication flaw; exploitation attempts reported; not in KEV
item.description: SonicWall published advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 on 6 October for CVE-2026-102255, a server-side request forgery in the Work Place interface of its SMA1000 remote-access appliances that it rates maximum severity; CISA’s enrichment scores it CVSS v3.1 10.0. Through an unintended alternate access path, an unauthenticated attacker can make the appliance send requests to its own internal functions. Affected are the SMA 6210, 7210 and 8200v on 12.4.3-03526 or older and 12.5.0-02952 or older; the fixes are 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082, and there is no workaround. The same release fixes three flaws that need authentication: an OS command injection (CVE-2026-102256), a Zip Slip in the Appliance Management Console (CVE-2026-102257) and stored cross-site scripting (CVE-2026-102258). SMA 100 appliances and firewall SSL VPN are not affected. Defused saw its first hits on SMA decoys on 8 October and Previdian counted 135 attempts from two US addresses; reporting so far describes attempts, not successful break-ins, and the flaw was still not in KEV as of CISA’s 30 October catalog. Some threat feeds now label it exploited, but that is a claim: no confirmed compromise has been reported, and CISA’s enrichment still records no exploitation. SMA1000 has been a repeated target this year, including zero-days exploited in June. No oil and gas victim is named. The sector read is ours: SMA1000 appliances broker vendor and contractor access into industrial networks, and a pre-authentication flaw on that broker is a direct line toward the OT DMZ. - SonicWall advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 and the CVE record (CISA-ADP CVSS); exploitation attempts as reported by SecurityWeek, The Hacker News and Dark Reading (12 Oct 2026); OT remote-access relevance is editorial assessment - Fix published 6 Oct 2026; attempts observed from 8 Oct 2026; reported 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA republishes Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory: GENESIS64 and GENESIS flaws up to CVSS 9.1 are fixed, but MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz will get no fix
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA/HMI and historian platform; CISA republication of 27 Oct; three older products get no fix; not exploited
item.description: On 27 October CISA republished Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory 2026-006, first issued by the vendor on 15 October, as ICSA-26-300-02. It covers four flaws in the ICONICS SCADA, HMI and historian line. CVE-2026-16438 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) concerns default DCOM permissions granted to the administrator account; CVE-2026-16436 (8.1) is an authentication bypass, in which a fixed challenge-response mechanism lets a remote attacker who obtains the response unlock any user account; CVE-2026-16437 (6.4) lets an administrator read and write the challenge-response file; and the libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (8.2) is also listed. The fixes are GENESIS 11.04, and 10.98 for GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and IoTWorX. MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz will not be fixed: Mitsubishi tells users to replace them and, in the meantime, to blank the challenge-response file and restrict write access to it. No exploitation of ICONICS products has been reported. None of the ICONICS-specific flaws is in KEV; the bundled libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 has been in KEV since 13 September 2023 from browser exploitation. The sector read is ours: platforms of this kind run in control rooms and on terminal and plant networks, and GENESIS32 and MC Works64 installations tend to stay in service long after support ends, so the republication is a useful prompt to find them. - Mitsubishi Electric PSIRT advisory 2026-006 (15 Oct 2026); CISA ICSA-26-300-02 (27 Oct 2026), CVSS v3.1 scores as listed there; libwebp KEV status per the CVE-2023-4863 record; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Vendor advisory 15 Oct 2026; CISA republication 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa: its Remote Connect client can be impersonated by an on-path attacker, and the end-of-life OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway carries static keys and an SMS command-injection flaw that will not be fixed
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client and end-of-life cellular gateway flaws; one product will not be fixed; not exploited
item.description: Moxa published two security advisories on 27 October. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, Moxa’s score) affects the MRC Client, the OpenVPN-based client for Moxa’s Remote Connect remote-access service, in versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0: it accepts a configuration supplied by the server without properly validating the certificate, so an attacker on the network path can impersonate the server. Version 4.2.2, obtained through Moxa support, fixes it. The OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway has two flaws: CVE-2026-111460 (7.7), static HTTPS and CA private keys built into the firmware, and CVE-2026-111461 (7.5), a command injection through the SMS-based upgrade feature. The gateway is end-of-life and will not be fixed; Moxa’s mitigations are to reset the device so that it generates new keys and to keep SMS disabled. Moxa also lists an authenticated denial-of-service flaw, CVE-2026-111548 (5.3), in NPort W2150A-W4 and W2250A-W4 wireless device servers. No exploitation is reported. The sector read is ours: cellular gateways of this kind carry RTU and flow-computer data from wellpads, tank batteries and meter stations, and remote-access clients are how vendors and engineers reach those sites, so both flaws sit on the remote-site edge. - Moxa security advisories MPSA-269510 and MPSA-261250 (27 Oct 2026), with CVE records via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; CVSS v4.0 per Moxa; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Published 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 20 October batch: a low-privileged user can get root on WAGO PFC and CC100 controllers, and Moxa’s AIG-302 edge gateway carries a hard-coded key — both fixed
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA ICS advisories of 20 Oct: controller command injection to root and an edge-gateway hard-coded key; fixed; not exploited
item.description: CISA published five ICS advisories on 20 October, and two bear on field automation. ICSA-26-293-02 republishes WAGO’s CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-096 for devices on WAGO’s Linux-based firmware below 4.10.0 (FW32): the CC100, PFC100 G2 and PFC200 G2 controllers, TP600 panels, Edge Controller and WP400. CVE-2026-80466 (CVSS v3.1 8.8) is an OS command injection through routing parameters in the web-based management interface, which a low-privileged remote user can use to have a root-owned helper run commands; CVE-2026-88850 (v3.1 8.1) is a missing authorisation check that lets low-privileged users change root-owned PROFIBUS parameters. Firmware 4.10.0 (FW32) fixes both. ICSA-26-293-03 covers Moxa’s AIG-302 gateways running ThingsPro Edge firmware 1.4.0 and earlier: CVE-2026-109813, a hard-coded cryptographic key (v3.1 8.1, v4.0 8.6), and CVE-2026-109812, a missing authorisation check (v3.1 6.8, v4.0 6.9), both fixed in 1.4.1. CISA lists energy among the sectors for both, and no exploitation is reported. The batch’s other three advisories cover PEAK-System CAN drivers and revisions to two Hitachi Energy power-grid notices. The sector read is ours: compact controllers like these are common in packaged equipment and remote facilities, and edge gateways are how field data leaves a site. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-293-02 (WAGO, republishing CERT@VDE VDE-2026-096) and ICSA-26-293-03 (Moxa), read via CISA’s CSAF records on CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; Moxa advisory MPSA-262560; deployment context is editorial assessment - CISA advisories published 20 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Schneider Electric: Sage RTUs do not properly verify firmware authenticity — and Pro-face and Harmony STW6 HMIs carry an 8.8 flaw triggered from a web page
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA RTU firmware authenticity and HMI component flaws; Schneider Electric October notices; not exploited
item.description: Schneider Electric issued two new security notices on 13 October. SEVD-2026-286-02 covers its Sage remote terminal units — the 1410, 1430, 1450, 2400, 3030 Magnum and 4400 — which do not sufficiently verify that firmware is authentic. Under CVE-2026-102250, modified firmware can be loaded when an authorised administrator starts an update; Schneider scores it CVSS v3.1 7.2 (v4.0 8.6) with high privileges required, and the fix is firmware C3414-500-S02L0. SEVD-2026-286-01 covers Pro-face STW6000 and Harmony STW6 HMIs, all versions, where an unmaintained third-party component could let an attacker take control of the device if a user visits a malicious web page; CVE-2026-96434 scores CVSS v3.1 8.8 and needs that user interaction. Schneider also reissued an older Altivar drive notice (SEVD-2025-252-01, version 5.0) the same day. Neither new flaw is in KEV and no exploitation is reported. The sector read is ours, and this one sits close to the sector: Sage RTUs are a long-standing choice for pipeline, gas-measurement and utility telemetry, so the realistic attack is a tampered firmware file reaching a technician’s laptop before an update visit — which makes the provenance of firmware as important as the patch. - Schneider Electric security notices SEVD-2026-286-01 and SEVD-2026-286-02 (13 Oct 2026), with CVE records via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Published 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] October OT Patch Tuesday: S7-1500 web-server flaws at CVSS 9.6 with no fix yet, an Industrial Edge path traversal, and an ArmorBlock password takeover
item.category: Critical Advisory — October OT Patch Tuesday: Siemens S7-1500, Industrial Edge and CROSSBOW, Rockwell ArmorBlock; several fixes not yet available; not exploited
item.description: Siemens released its October advisories on 13 October; SecurityWeek counts 17. Three matter most for process plants. SSA-591731 covers eight web-server flaws (CVE-2026-63350 to -63357) in S7-1500, ET 200SP, ET 200pro and Drive Controller CPUs, all versions, that could let an attacker run code in an authorised user’s browser and carry out PLC operations with that user’s rights; Siemens scores the advisory CVSS v3.1 9.6 and has no fix yet, only mitigations. SSA-784472 lists 377 CVEs, up to CVSS 10.0, in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP technology module — the module, not the CPUs — again with no fix yet. SSA-832641 is an authenticated path traversal in Industrial Edge devices and some HMI panels (CVE-2026-44415, CVSS 9.1), fixed for Edge devices, IoT2050 and IPCs but not yet for SCALANCE LPE9413/9433 or the affected panels. Siemens also fixed 11 flaws, up to CVSS 8.8, in RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW in version 6.0. Rockwell’s only new advisory, SD1801, covers 1732E ArmorBlock I/O modules on 3.012 and earlier: CVE-2026-12655 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) lets an unauthenticated attacker change the web-server password and take over the module, and CVE-2026-12656 (7.5) is a traffic-flood denial of service that needs a power cycle to clear; 3.013 fixes both and there is no workaround. Nothing in the set is in KEV or reported exploited. CISA republished the Siemens advisories on 22 October as ICSA-26-295-02 to -18, and the S7 web-server flaws and the S7-1500 MFP Linux-subsystem issues still had no fix. The sector read is ours: S7-1500 controllers and ArmorBlock I/O arrive inside compressor packages, terminal loading systems and vendor skids, which is where version tracking tends to fail. - Siemens ProductCERT advisories SSA-591731, SSA-784472, SSA-832641 and SSA-508506; Rockwell Automation advisory SD1801; advisory count per SecurityWeek’s 14 Oct 2026 roundup; CISA republications ICSA-26-295-02 to -18 (22 Oct 2026); oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Siemens and Rockwell advisories 13 Oct 2026; SecurityWeek roundup 14 Oct 2026; CISA republished the Siemens set 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA: an authorisation flaw in Inductive Automation Ignition lets users escalate their privileges — CVSS 8.8, fixed in 8.1.55 and 8.3.9
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA/HMI platform privilege escalation; CISA ICS advisory; not exploited
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-286-01 on 13 October for Inductive Automation’s Ignition SCADA and HMI platform. CVE-2026-92817 is an incorrect-authorisation flaw that allows privilege escalation, scored CVSS v3.1 8.8 (v4.0 8.7). Ignition 8.1.0 to 8.1.54 and 8.3.0 to 8.3.8 are affected, and 8.1.55 and 8.3.9 fix it. CISA reports no known public exploitation, the flaw is not in KEV, and the advisory lists the Critical Manufacturing, Energy and Information Technology sectors. It was one of two advisories CISA issued that day; the other covered a consumer Wi-Fi camera. The sector read is ours: Ignition is widely used for production monitoring, pipeline and gathering-system SCADA, terminal HMIs and the dashboards that pull data from all three, and privilege escalation on a SCADA gateway is how a stolen low-level login becomes more control than it should ever have had. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-286-01 (CSAF record as indexed by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup), corroborated by SecurityWeek; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Advisory published 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] A second critical lwIP flaw in two weeks: CISA flags a CVSS 9.8 buffer overflow in the SMTP client, after September’s MQTT client bug — exposure depends on each device vendor
item.category: Critical Advisory — Embedded TCP/IP stack; two critical client flaws in two weeks; exposure set by each device vendor
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-279-02 on 6 October for the SMTP client in lwIP 2.2.1, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack built into many controllers, gateways and sensors. CVE-2026-15340 is a classic buffer overflow that the advisory scores CVSS v3.1 9.8 (v4.0 9.3 in the CVE record). The fix is an upstream patch and commit rather than a new release, and CISA lists the Energy and Water and Wastewater sectors. It follows ICSA-26-265-01 of 22 September for lwIP’s MQTT client, CVE-2026-87121, an out-of-bounds write also scored 9.8 that may allow full code execution on the device; that batch also carried a second lwIP advisory, six Siemens republications and OpenPLC Runtime v3. Neither lwIP flaw is reported exploited or listed in KEV. Both sit in optional client applications inside a library, so whether a given RTU, flow computer, gas detector or wireless gateway is affected depends on whether its maker built in the SMTP or MQTT client — something only the device vendors can answer.
