Devices that email alarms or reports, or publish telemetry over MQTT, are the ones to ask about first. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-279-02 (6 Oct 2026) and ICSA-26-265-01 to -09 (22 Sep 2026), via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup and CISA’s CSAF files; CVSS per the advisories and CVE records; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - MQTT client advisory 22 Sep 2026; SMTP client advisory 6 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] An exploited FortiMail flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the mail gateway — in KEV since 1 October, and Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited email security gateway, CISA KEV
item.description: Fortinet published FG-IR-26-175 on 1 October for CVE-2026-104286, a path traversal flaw combined with improper NULL-byte handling in FortiMail. Fortinet says it lets an unauthenticated attacker “write arbitrary files on the underlying system via crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests”, scores it CVSS 9.8 and says it has been reported exploited in the wild; Fortinet found the flaw internally. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 4 October federal deadline. Affected branches are 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1. When the advisory first appeared the fixed releases were listed as planned, with no date. Fortinet’s 5 October update now lists 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2 or later, and tells 7.2 users to move to the 7.4 branch or above. Its workarounds still matter until each unit is upgraded: disable Identity-Based Encryption (IBE), restrict webmail access from untrusted networks, and use web application firewall rules to block path-traversal requests to the IBE endpoint. No actor, campaign or victim has been disclosed. The sector read is ours: a mail gateway is not OT, but in oil and gas it is the relay for vendor advisories, nominations and scheduling, and the alarm and production-report email that leaves plant networks, and a file-write foothold on it is a trusted position next to the systems the business side of operations depends on. - Fortinet PSIRT advisory FG-IR-26-175 and its 5 Oct solution update; CISA KEV entry; launch-day fix status as reported by SecurityWeek; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Advisory and KEV addition 1 Oct 2026 (due 4 Oct); fixed releases listed 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: an exploited authentication bypass gives unauthenticated attackers admin-level API access to the system that configures every site — CVSS 9.8, in KEV since 30 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited SD-WAN management controller, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-76504 on 30 September. Improper handling of URI encoding in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager lets a remote, unauthenticated request get past an authentication rule meant to restrict a specific API endpoint, giving administrator-level access. Cisco scores it CVSS 9.8, says there are no workarounds, and states that its PSIRT “became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability” in September 2026. CISA added it to KEV on 30 September with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised the advisory to version 1.1 on 2 October. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1; releases older than 20.9 must migrate to a fixed release. BleepingComputer counts it as the fifth exploited Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. No actor or victim has been named. The sector read is ours: where SD-WAN carries traffic between control centres, compressor and pump stations, terminals and field offices, the manager is the system that pushes configuration and policy to every edge router, so admin access to it is a route to changing segmentation at every site at once. It is the same exposure as the Arista VeloCloud orchestrator, where a third exploited flaw was patched on 22 October (see Arista VeloCloud). - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU (v1.1); CISA KEV entry; zero-day count per BleepingComputer; oil and gas WAN relevance is editorial assessment - Advisory and KEV addition 30 Sep 2026 (due 3 Oct); advisory revised 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA 2030: the agency’s four-year strategy puts OT visibility and consequence-based prioritisation at its centre — a direction, not a new requirement
item.category: Policy — CISA four-year strategy naming OT protection and consequence-based prioritisation; no new obligations
item.description: CISA released “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail” on 26 October. It has three pillars. Defend includes an objective to protect operational technology — modernising OT environments and improving asset visibility and anomaly detection — alongside supply-chain integrity; Harden is about turning intelligence into faster operational action; and Prevail covers resilience, ten regional offices and emergency communications. CISA says it will move away from threat-agnostic, all-hazards approaches toward risk-informed, consequence-based analysis and will support a national risk register. The timetable is a review of core services starting within 60 days, an implementation plan with metrics within 180 days, and a progress update after a year. The strategy creates no new legal authorities and no obligations for operators. Analysts quoted by GovInfoSecurity question how much the agency can deliver after losing about a third of its staff. The read for oil and gas is ours: consequence-based prioritisation is the logic pipeline and refinery operators already apply to their own assets, and the core-services review is worth watching for changes to the assessments and advisory support operators use. - CISA 2030 strategy as reported by Cybersecurity Dive and Nextgov/FCW (26 Oct 2026); analysts’ views via GovInfoSecurity; oil and gas reading is editorial - Released 26 Oct 2026; core-services review to begin within 60 days

item.title: [Info] Coast Guard NVIC 02-26 sets out how vessels, port facilities and Outer Continental Shelf facilities should build the cyber plans due by 16 July 2027 — penetration testing is not required for the first plan
item.category: Guidance — Coast Guard implementation guidance for the maritime cyber rule; covers Outer Continental Shelf facilities; plans due 16 Jul 2027
item.description: The US Coast Guard has issued Navigation and Vessel Inspection Circular 02-26, its guidance on meeting the cybersecurity requirements of 33 CFR Part 101 Subpart F, the maritime cyber rule. Industrial Cyber reported it on 23 October; the Coast Guard’s file name dates it 19 October. It applies to US-flagged vessels, MTSA-regulated facilities and Outer Continental Shelf facilities, and walks through designating a qualified Cybersecurity Officer, carrying out the Cybersecurity Assessment and writing the Cybersecurity Plan, including identifying critical IT and OT systems and how they depend on each other. All three are due to the Coast Guard by 16 July 2027. Penetration testing is not required for the first plan; an enclosure sets out expectations, including OT safety, for the five-year renewal cycle, and another offers an optional method based on the NIST Cybersecurity Framework for scoping critical systems. The approach is performance-based: the Coast Guard does not prescribe products or require third-party assessors. An NVIC explains how to comply; it does not change the rule’s deadlines. The fit for this page is direct for offshore facilities on the Outer Continental Shelf and, in our reading, for the marine oil, fuel and LNG terminals that are MTSA-regulated facilities (editorial assessment). - US Coast Guard NVIC 02-26 as reported by Industrial Cyber (23 Oct 2026); issue date inferred from the Coast Guard file name; the circular itself was not retrieved; oil and gas terminal fit is editorial assessment - Dated 19 Oct 2026 (per file name); reported 23 Oct 2026; plans due 16 Jul 2027

item.title: [Info] A maritime coalition launches a vulnerability repository for ship and port IT and OT — a reference point for the ship-shore interface at energy terminals
item.category: Programme — Industry vulnerability database for ship and port IT and OT; a resource, not a threat
item.description: A coalition calling itself the Blue Initiative — the maritime security firms Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, the classification societies Bureau Veritas and ClassNK, and MTS-ISAC — launched the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository on or before 26 October. It gathers IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to vessels and port systems, reviewed by Cydome and partner researchers before publication, and lets users filter by equipment or vendor, read analyst notes and subscribe to alerts. Infosecurity Magazine reports that entries are published only once a patch is available, and Cydome’s chief executive describes it as a public and open single source of truth for maritime vulnerabilities. Infosecurity gives no entry counts; figures circulating elsewhere could not be verified and are not repeated here. The fit for this page is editorial: terminal operators already question vessel owners about shipboard security (see the tanker card), and a shared catalogue of shipboard and port flaws gives those conversations something concrete to check against. - Blue Initiative launch as reported by Infosecurity Magazine (26 Oct 2026), also covered by SecurityWeek; entry counts not verified and omitted; oil and gas terminal relevance is editorial assessment - Launched on or before 26 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] Accenture, Dragos and SANS launch a foundation offering free OT monitoring, deployment and training to up to 500 small utilities — natural gas utilities are eligible, and enrolment opens soon
item.category: Programme — Free OT monitoring, deployment and training for small utilities, natural gas included; private funding, no new requirement
item.description: On 20 October Accenture, Dragos and the SANS Institute launched the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation, a nonprofit with about US$10 million in initial funding and services, with Elastic providing technology support. Its first phase covers up to 500 utilities with annual revenue under US$100 million, on top of the more than 100 already in Dragos’s Community Defense Program. Participants get Dragos Platform access, Neighborhood Keeper and Dragos’s OT-CERT; assessment, deployment, configuration and ongoing support from Accenture; SANS OnDemand training with GIAC certification; and hardware funding where needed. The foundation’s site lists electric, natural gas, water and wastewater utilities in the US and Canada, while Dragos’s announcement speaks of US utilities; enrolment “opens soon”, with an interest list in the meantime. There is no government involvement. “Access was never the problem. Knowing help was available and adoption was,” Dragos’s Robert M. Lee wrote. For this sector the fit is municipal and small investor-owned gas distribution systems, which run SCADA, gate, regulator and odorisation stations with few security staff (editorial assessment). - Dragos announcement (20 Oct 2026) and the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation website; government involvement per The Record (21 Oct 2026); natural gas fit is editorial assessment - Announced 20 Oct 2026; enrolment not yet open

item.title: [Info] The OT Cybersecurity Coalition presses CISA again for a binding directive on federal agencies’ own OT, now citing the French refrigeration attack — a proposal, not a CISA action
item.category: Policy — Industry proposal for a federal OT directive, renewed after the French attack; no CISA action
item.description: CyberScoop reported on 6 October that the OT Cybersecurity Coalition has published a paper urging CISA to issue a Binding Operational Directive focused solely on operational technology at federal civilian agencies. The coalition wants the directive to assign responsibility at each agency, including an accountable OT cybersecurity officer, set minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, align with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and consider whether NSA’s OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. In its words, “it is time for an encompassing BOD solely focused on OT security.” Earlier directives touched OT without being built for it. CISA did not respond to CyberScoop and has announced no directive. The paper leans on GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September: of 22 civilian CFO Act agencies reviewed, 15 had established inventories of networked IoT and OT devices, 11 maintained them, 10 included all required information, and only 7 met all three OMB requirements. GAO’s one recommendation is that OMB issue updated guidance covering these devices and oversee implementation. A directive would bind federal agencies only; the coalition’s argument is that it would also signal to the private sector what the government expects. On 14 October the coalition returned to the subject after the French supermarket refrigeration attack: in a statement reported by Industrial Cyber, it said failures in cybersecurity fundamentals had led to a significant incident, repeated ANSSI’s advice on VPN-only remote access, default passwords and firmware, renewed its call for a binding OT directive, and warned that refrigeration controllers could become an attack vector in the United States too, while noting that no US incidents have been reported. For oil and gas operators the practical value today is GAO’s three tests, which work as a self-check on your own OT asset inventory. - OT Cybersecurity Coalition paper as reported by CyberScoop (6 Oct 2026); coalition statement of 14 Oct 2026 as reported by Industrial Cyber (16 Oct 2026); GAO-26-108937; no OT-specific CISA directive found as of 28 Oct 2026 - GAO report published 30 Sep 2026; coalition proposal reported 6 Oct 2026; follow-up statement 14 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] GAO: industry panelists, energy among them, say overlapping federal cyber rules are hard to satisfy while fighting an incident — and the CIRCIA final rule is now under White House review
item.category: Policy — Federal incident reporting; GAO report, no new requirement
item.description: The Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-109197, “Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them”, on 28 September. It records a virtual panel held on 16 July with six industry representatives from the energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health sectors. Panelists said it could be difficult to meet every reporting requirement while also remediating a cyber threat, saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector-specific ones, and half of them agreed that progress on harmonisation has been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency, such as CISA, to coordinate reporting; and more collaboration between government and industry. Cybersecurity Dive reports that energy participants named TSA pipeline reporting and NERC CIP among the overlapping regimes. The report makes no formal GAO recommendations. It adds to a count already in circulation: on 8 September the McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, drawing on GAO work, tallied 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. The rule most likely to change the picture has not arrived. CISA has now sent its CIRCIA final rule to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, which logged it for review on 1 October; the text is not public, the statutory deadline passed a year ago, and HIPAA Journal reports publication is expected before year-end. Once in force, covered incidents are to be reported within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24, from dates the final rule sets. Oil and gas operators will recognise the problem: one event can trigger TSA pipeline security directive reporting to CISA, Coast Guard reporting for regulated terminals, SEC disclosure, state regulators, insurers and contractual notices. - GAO-26-109197, with coverage by Cybersecurity Dive and Industrial Cyber; McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis as reported by Industrial Cyber; CIRCIA status from the reginfo.gov regulatory review record and HIPAA Journal - McCrary analysis 8 Sep 2026; GAO report published 28 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule received for OIRA review 1 Oct 2026; no publication found as of 28 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s “Securing the Next 250” campaign: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, recover quickly — voluntary, but the end-of-support message lands on the field edge
item.category: Policy — CISA awareness campaign; voluntary, no new requirement
item.description: CISA has launched “Securing the Next 250” for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, as reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. It is built around three Rs: Reduce attack surfaces, Replace end-of-support devices, and Recover quickly to sustain operations. Acting Director Nick Andersen framed it around dependency: when critical infrastructure is disrupted, “so are the businesses and communities that depend on vital services.” Beyond the three Rs the campaign promotes logging, backing up and encrypting data, reporting incidents to CISA, and keeping an incident response plan that is exercised, with realistic drills that include leadership and legal counsel at least once a year, and it singles out replacing end-of-support edge devices. It is guidance and promotion, not a requirement. The fit for oil and gas is editorial but direct: this edition’s exploited edge flaws — PAN-OS and Cisco ASA firewalls, Citrix and Ivanti gateways, Cisco SD-WAN and FortiMail — are the class of device the Replace message is aimed at, ABB’s obsolete Arctic gateways will get no PHP2Shell fix at all, and remote sites are where routers, gateways and switches tend to outlive their vendor support. - CISA campaign as reported by Industrial Cyber; oil and gas framing is editorial - Reported 2 Oct 2026
